subject: Pathology
vignette: A 25-year-old woman with darkly pigmented skin has an earlobe piercing that heals with a firm, raised nodule extending well beyond the original puncture site. The lesion has clawlike projections into adjacent normal tissue. Her mother had a similar lesion after a shoulder injury.
question: Which of the following best distinguishes this lesion from a hypertrophic scar?

options.text: The scar remains confined to the original wound borders
The scar contains parallel collagen bundles with increased type III collagen only
The scar recurs infrequently after excision and has no familial predisposition
The scar extends beyond the borders of the original wound with disorganized collagen
The scar forms only after infected wounds and never on the earlobe

explanation_correct: A keloid extends beyond the borders of the original wound, has clawlike projections, and shows disorganized collagen with greatly increased synthesis of types I and III collagen. It typically occurs on earlobes, face, and upper extremities, recurs frequently after excision, and has increased incidence in people with darker skin. A hypertrophic scar instead stays within the wound borders, has parallel collagen organization, and recurs infrequently.

explanation_incorrect.A: Confinement to the original wound borders describes a hypertrophic scar, which is the lesion this patient does not have.
explanation_incorrect.B: Parallel collagen bundles are a feature of hypertrophic scar, and keloids show a far greater increase affecting both type I and type III collagen rather than type III alone.
explanation_incorrect.C: Keloids recur frequently and are more common in people with darker skin, so this describes the opposite of the keloid pattern.
explanation_incorrect.E: Earlobe keloids are among the classic sites listed, and keloid formation does not require preceding wound infection.

educationalObjective: A keloid extends beyond the original wound with disorganized predominantly type I and III collagen and recurs frequently, unlike a hypertrophic scar.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 40-year-old man sustains a full-thickness burn over the anterior chest and left axilla. Six months after grafting, the healed area is tight and shiny, and he cannot fully raise his left arm because the scar tissue has shortened across the axillary fold.
question: Which of the following best describes this complication?

options.text: Keloid formation with extension beyond the original wound
Hypertrophic scar confined to the wound borders with parallel collagen
Dehiscence of the wound with separation of the edges
Wound contracture from scar contraction limiting joint mobility
Proud flesh with excessive granulation tissue above the skin surface

explanation_correct: Scar formation replaces nonregenerated tissue when repair cannot be accomplished by regeneration alone, and when that fibrous tissue shortens across an overlying joint it produces a contracture that restricts mobility. Wound contraction during the proliferative phase is mediated by myofibroblasts and is beneficial in closing defects, but excessive contraction across a joint or a body orifice becomes a functional impairment. This is why deep burns crossing joints receive splinting and early grafting.

explanation_incorrect.A: A keloid is a raised scar that extends beyond the wound with clawlike projections, which is a cosmetic and symptomatic problem rather than the mechanical restriction described here.
explanation_incorrect.B: A hypertrophic scar is bulky but stays within the wound borders and does not produce the tight shortening across the axillary fold.
explanation_incorrect.C: Dehiscence is rupture of a wound along a surgical incision, typically early in healing, and does not describe a mature tight scar.
explanation_incorrect.E: Proud flesh refers to excessive granulation tissue that protrudes above the wound surface and blocks epithelialization, not to fibrous shortening.

educationalObjective: Contracture is excessive scar contraction that shortens tissue across a joint or orifice and restricts mobility.

subject: Pathology
vignette: An 8-year-old boy has a surgical incision closed with heavy sutures over a rapidly healing wound, and the surgeon notes at a follow-up visit that a friable, red, fleshy mass of tissue protrudes above the level of the surrounding skin. The wound edges have not re-epithelialized over it.
question: Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this finding?

options.text: Excessive collagen synthesis with disorganized bundles extending beyond the wound
Separation of the wound edges from failure of suture material
Fibrous shortening of the scar across a joint space
Excessive production of granulation tissue, called proud flesh, that protrudes above the skin surface
Deposition of type I collagen replacing type III collagen too early

explanation_correct: Proud flesh is the clinical term for excessive granulation tissue that rises above the surface of the wound and delays epithelial coverage, appearing as a red, granular, friable mass. Granulation tissue is normally deposited during the proliferative phase under the influence of fibroblast growth factor, vascular endothelial growth factor, and platelet-derived growth factor, and when this deposition overshoots the defect the tissue protrudes. Removing the excess tissue allows epithelialization to proceed, because epithelium cannot migrate across the raised mass.

explanation_incorrect.A: Disorganized collagen extending beyond the wound borders describes a keloid, which is a mature scar rather than a friable red mass of granulation tissue.
explanation_incorrect.B: Separation of wound edges is dehiscence, which presents as an open wound or evisceration, not as tissue protruding above an intact surface.
explanation_incorrect.C: Fibrous shortening across a joint is a contracture producing a functional deficit in range of motion.
explanation_incorrect.E: The switch from type III to type I collagen occurs in remodeling and increases tensile strength; it does not produce a protruding granulation mass.

educationalObjective: Proud flesh is excessive granulation tissue protruding above the wound surface, which prevents epithelialization and must be removed.
